title: "How it was tested"
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("R/_site_helpers.R")
```

Three quantities, measured annually for each jurisdiction from 1997 to 2019:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Emissions** | greenhouse gases, kilotonnes of CO₂ equivalent |
| **Energy** | industrial energy use, terajoules |
| **Output** | real GDP, millions of chained 2012 dollars |

All three are used in logarithms, so coefficients read as proportional changes.

## The problem these tests solve

Two series that both rise over time will look related whether or not they have anything
to do with each other. Canadian GDP rose from 1997 to 2019; so did the global population
of house cats. A naive regression would find them strongly associated.

Econometrics calls this a **spurious regression**, and the whole testing sequence below
exists to avoid it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The technical version

A series with a *unit root* has no tendency to return to any particular level: shocks
persist indefinitely, and its variance grows without bound. Regressing one such series on
another produces high R² and significant t-statistics even when the two are independent,
because conventional standard errors are invalid.

The fix is *cointegration*. If two non-stationary series are tied together by some
long-run equilibrium, a particular linear combination of them will be stationary even
though neither is. Finding such a combination is evidence of a genuine relationship
rather than a shared trend.
:::

## The sequence

### 1. Is each series non-stationary?

An **augmented Dickey-Fuller** test asks whether a series wanders without returning to a
central value. Every one of the 33 series tested here does. After taking year-to-year
differences, 27 of 33 settle down — the standard pattern, and the precondition for
everything that follows.

### 2. Do they share a long-run relationship?

Two tests, which is where it gets interesting, because **they are not testing the same
model**.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Engle-Granger

Fits one equation —

$$\ln \text{GHG} = \alpha + \beta t + \gamma \ln \text{GDP} + \delta (\ln \text{GDP})^2 + \theta \ln \text{ENC} + u$$

— and tests whether its residuals are stationary. If they are, the variables are tied
together.

The squared GDP term carries the *environmental Kuznets curve*: the hypothesis that
emissions rise with income, then fall once a country is rich enough to afford cleaner
technology. Including it is what makes this the EKC specification.

## Johansen

Treats the three variables as a system and asks how many independent long-run
relationships — the *cointegrating rank* — hold among them. The rank can be 0 (no
relationship), 1, or 2.

A rank of 3, the number of variables, is a special case worth naming: it means the system
is stationary in levels, so there is nothing to cointegrate. **Full rank is not strong
cointegration. It is the absence of it.**

The squared term cannot appear here. $(\ln \text{GDP})^2$ is not a linear transformation
of $\ln \text{GDP}$, and this method requires a linear system.
:::

That difference is the main reason the two disagree. One tests the EKC relationship; the
other tests a relationship without the turning point. They answer different questions, and
reporting both is more honest than picking one.

### 3. Does one predict another?

**Granger causality** asks whether past values of one series improve forecasts of
another, beyond what the second series' own history already provides.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This is prediction, not causation. A variable can Granger-cause another through a common
driver neither of them controls. The name is unfortunate and has misled people for fifty
years.
:::

When the underlying series are non-stationary, the standard test is unreliable. The
**Toda-Yamamoto** procedure fixes this by deliberately over-fitting the model with extra
lags and then testing only the original ones, which restores the test's distribution.
That correction matters here — see the [reproduction page](reproduction.qmd).

### 4. Are the residuals well behaved?

**Breusch-Godfrey** for autocorrelation, **Breusch-Pagan** for changing error variance.
Both are run on the single equation above.

## Why the answers are fragile

Every test above needs a choice of **lag order** — how far back the model looks. With 23
observations, nothing in the data settles that choice:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lag
#| tbl-cap: "Parameters per equation against usable observations, for the three-variable system."
tibble(
  `lag order` = 2:4,
  `parameters per equation` = 3 * (2:4) + 2,
  `usable observations` = 23 - (2:4),
  `residual d.f.` = (23 - (2:4)) - (3 * (2:4) + 2)
)
```

At four lags the model fits 14 parameters to 19 observations. The standard selection
criteria split: Akaike's picks four lags in ten of eleven jurisdictions, Schwarz's picks
one in nine of eleven. Rather than choose, the analysis reports every answer.
